readerTitle: Why the same company looked brilliant, then arrogant
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Cisco, Rosenzweig의 분석) + 실제 연구 (Thorndike 1920, Nisbett & Wilson 1977) + 가상 적용 (IT 지원 업체 선정, 주방 리모델링 업체)
insight: 하나의 강한 인상(성과, 매력, 세련됨)은 무관한 자질의 평가까지 물들인다. 그래서 자질은 따로따로, 결과를 보기 전에 판단해야 한다.
misconception: 잘나가는 회사나 인상 좋은 사람은 다른 면도 당연히 훌륭할 것이다. 그리고 나는 그런 인상에 흔들리지 않는다.

sources.text: Rosenzweig, P. (2007). The Halo Effect... and the Eight Other Business Delusions That Deceive Managers. Free Press.
Thorndike, E. L. (1920). A constant error in psychological ratings. Journal of Applied Psychology, 4(1), 25–29.
Nisbett, R. E., & Wilson, T. D. (1977). The halo effect: Evidence for unconscious alteration of judgments. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 35(4), 250–256.

factChecks.note: Cisco가 2000년 3월 잠시 시가총액 세계 1위였다는 점, 2001년 매출 급감과 대규모 재고 상각이 있었다는 점을 게시 전 재확인하세요. 카드에는 구체 금액 없이 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
Rosenzweig가 Cisco 언론 보도를 예로 들어 같은 특성(문화, 리더십, 인수 전략)이 호황기에는 칭찬, 침체기에는 비판받았다고 분석한 내용을 책 원문으로 확인하세요. 직접 인용은 쓰지 않았습니다. 책 부제의 숫자(Eight/Nine Other) 표기도 확인 필요.
Thorndike(1920) 연구 대상이 군 장교들의 부하 평가였고, 서로 다른 자질 점수 간 상관이 지나치게 높았다는 요약이 맞는지 확인하세요.
Nisbett & Wilson(1977): 같은 강사가 따뜻하게/차갑게 행동하는 영상을 본 학생들이 외모, 버릇, 억양을 다르게 평가했고, 참가자들은 그 영향을 부인했다는 요약을 원문으로 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why the same company looked brilliant, then arrogant
body: In 2000, Cisco was briefly the most valuable company in the world. Writers praised its culture, its leaders and its smart acquisitions.
Then the tech market crashed and Cisco's sales fell hard. Soon many of the same traits were described as flaws. The company hadn't changed much. The results had.

image.label: One office building drawn twice: glowing, then grey
image.brief: 같은 사무실 건물을 좌우로 두 번 그림. 왼쪽은 금빛 후광과 박수 이모지, 오른쪽은 회색 비구름과 엄지 내림. 건물 자체는 완전히 동일하게. 실제 기업 로고나 이름은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Two IT support firms want your contract.
body: Firm A gives a stunning pitch in a sleek office. The founder is charming and mentions a famous client.
Firm B's pitch is plain. They hand over a sheet of response times and a list of client references.
You need a firm that fixes problems fast for a 40-person company. What do you do?

options.text: Pick Firm A. A team this polished probably runs support well too
options.feedback: Pitching well and fixing servers at 2 a.m. are different skills. You'd be paying for the second based on evidence of the first.

options.text: Ask both for the same proof: references your size, response records, and who does the actual work
options.feedback: It costs a week of calls, but it judges each firm on the skill you're buying, not on the impression it made.

options.text: Pick Firm B. A plain pitch suggests they focus on the work
options.feedback: Their data is a good sign. But "plain means honest" is also a shortcut from one trait to another. Check it.

cards.title: The story followed the stock price.
body: Business professor Phil Rosenzweig studied how the press described Cisco before and after the crash.
On the way up, its focus on customers and its fast acquisitions were signs of genius. On the way down, writers found sloppy control and arrogance in much the same company.
His point: people saw strong results, then **read those results back** into the culture and leadership. The judgment of the parts came from the judgment of the whole.

cards.title: The halo effect
body: The **halo effect** is when one strong impression spills over into how we judge other, unrelated qualities.
Good results make leaders look wise. A warm smile makes a pitch sound smart. It works in reverse too: one bad trait can darken everything else. This is sometimes called the *horns effect*.

image.label: One bright trait lighting up the traits around it
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 큰 원 "Great results"에서 빛이 퍼져 주변 작은 원들 "Leadership", "Culture", "Strategy", "Honesty"까지 같은 색으로 물드는 모습. 작은 원들 위에 "never measured" 작은 라벨.

cards.title: We don't notice it happening.
body: In 1920, psychologist Edward Thorndike looked at how military officers rated their soldiers. Scores for very different traits, like physique, intelligence and leadership, moved together far more than they should have.

In a 1977 study, students watched the same lecturer acting either warm or cold. Those who saw the warm version rated his looks, mannerisms and accent more favorably. Most insisted his warmth had **not affected** those ratings.

cards.title: Halos form wherever one thing is easy to see.
list: **A star salesperson:** their opinions on hiring or product get extra weight
**A tidy shop:** customers assume the food is fresher
**A famous client:** a supplier seems reliable in work you never saw
**One bad meeting:** a new manager seems weak at everything
cards.callout: The visible trait sets the tone. The hidden ones get filled in to match.
cards.softwareNote: A beautiful interface makes users assume the product is also secure and reliable. And when a startup grows fast, founders copy its every habit, as if each one caused the growth.

cards.title: Sometimes the halo is earned.
body: Good traits do often come together. A firm that does great work may really be well run. The mistake is treating one trait as proof of another without checking.

Knowing about the bias doesn't switch it off. The students in 1977 couldn't see it in themselves. What helps is structure: judge each quality separately, with its own evidence, and where you can, before you see the overall result.

cards.title: Now it's a kitchen renovation.
body: A contractor arrives right on time, friendly and well dressed. The portfolio photos are gorgeous. The quote is in the middle of three bids.
You're ready to sign. What do you do first?

options.text: Sign now. This level of professionalism shows in the work
options.feedback: Punctuality and good photos are real, but they say little about staying on budget or the quality of hidden plumbing.

options.text: Call two past clients about budget and schedule, check insurance, and ask who does the plumbing and wiring
options.feedback: A few calls delay the start slightly. In return you judge the things that cost the most when they go wrong.

options.text: Pick the cheapest bid so charm can't sway you
options.feedback: It avoids one halo but swaps in another shortcut: price. You still know nothing about the quality of the work.

cards.title: One bright trait is not evidence for the rest.
body: When someone or something impresses you, name the quality that impressed you. Then ask what evidence you have for each of the others.
**Try it today:** think of a supplier, hire or partner you admire. List three qualities you rely on them for. Mark which ones you've actually seen proof of.
